name: Portugal
traditionNote: A codified civil-law system of the Franco-Germanic line: the Civil Code of 1966 and its siblings are the starting point, and while the binding assento was abolished as unconstitutional, the Supreme Court's acórdãos de uniformização de jurisprudência still do much of the work of settling a disputed reading.
summary: Portugal legislates from two places at once. The Assembleia da República passes leis, and the Government makes decretos-leis — either in its own reserved competence, or under a legislative authorisation from the Assembly, or to develop the framework of a lei de bases. Both go to the President of the Republic, who promulgates, vetoes, or refers the text to the Constitutional Court for preventive review before it can be published at all. Publication in the Diário da República, 1.ª série, is what gives a diploma force; under the Act on the publication of legal instruments a text that fixes no date of its own enters into force on the fifth day after publication in the mainland. The 2.ª série carries the acts of the administration — ministerial despatches, appointments, university and agency statutes, regulations of public bodies. The electronic edition has been the only official one since 2006, and the whole gazette is now free to read without an account or a subscription. The two autonomous regions, the Azores and Madeira, have their own legislative assemblies whose decretos legislativos regionais are published both in the Diário da República and in the region's own official journal.
hierarchy: Constituição da República Portuguesa (1976), including the rights, freedoms and guarantees that bind public and private entities directly
EU law and international law — general or common international law and duly ratified conventions, which under Article 8 apply internally
Lei and decreto-lei — statutes of the Assembly and legislative decrees of the Government, of equal rank save where the Constitution reserves a matter to one of them
Decreto legislativo regional — legislative decrees of the Azores and Madeira within the regions' matters
Decreto regulamentar, portaria and despacho normativo — government regulations in descending order of formality
Regulamentos of independent authorities and public bodies, published mostly in the 2.ª série
Regulamentos and posturas municipais — municipal regulations, published locally and in the municipal edital

gazette.name: Diario da Republica
gazette.authority: Imprensa Nacional-Casa da Moeda, under the Ministry of the Presidency
gazette.coverage: Daily, in two series; the electronic edition has been the only official one since 2006, with the printed edition discontinued and the archive of earlier issues digitised
gazette.desc: The gazette in which Portuguese law is published and takes force. The 1.ª série carries the Constitution and its amendments, statutes, legislative decrees, regional legislative decrees, treaties, regulatory decrees and the Constitutional Court rulings with general binding force; the 2.ª série carries the acts of the administration. Which series a text appears in is itself a statement about its rank.
gazette.howto: Use the search at diariodarepublica.pt/dr/pesquisa, filtering by series, date, type of diploma and issuing body; a diploma opens at a stable address of the form /dr/detalhe/<slug>/<id>. The consolidated version of a diploma, where one exists, sits at /dr/legislacao-consolidada/<slug>/<id> and is reachable from the diploma's own page.
gazette.note: A diploma that fixes no date of entry into force takes effect on the fifth day after publication in the mainland, with longer periods for the autonomous regions and abroad — the date of publication is rarely the date the rule bites.

constitution.name: Constituicao da Republica Portuguesa
constitution.authority: Assembleia Constituinte, 2 April 1976; published in the Diário da República and maintained in consolidated form there
constitution.coverage: In force since 25 April 1976 and revised seven times, most recently in 2005; the consolidated text shows the current wording with its revision history
constitution.desc: A long constitution born of the 1974 revolution, with an extensive catalogue of rights, freedoms and guarantees that bind public and private entities directly, a semi-presidential structure, and a Constitutional Court with preventive, abstract and concrete review powers — including review of unconstitutionality by omission.
constitution.howto: Read the consolidated text article by article on the DRE; the Assembly publishes an English translation of the seventh revision as a PDF on parlamento.pt, alongside French and Spanish versions.
constitution.note: Revision requires a two-thirds majority of members in office and must respect the entrenched limits in Article 288, which include the republican form, the unitary state with the regional autonomies, and the separation of church and state.

sources.name: Legislacao consolidada (DRE)
sources.authority: Imprensa Nacional-Casa da Moeda / Diário da República Eletrónico
sources.coverage: The major diplomas and a growing body of others, with amendments incorporated and each version dated; not every diploma has a consolidated version
sources.desc: The working text of a Portuguese diploma with its amendments merged in, published by the gazette itself. Each consolidated text records the amending diplomas against the articles they changed, so the history is readable from the text rather than reconstructed.
sources.howto: Search for the diploma and take the consolidated version from its page where one is offered; the URL form is /dr/legislacao-consolidada/<slug>/<id>. Where no consolidated version exists — and for many older or minor diplomas there is none — you must read the original and every amending diploma in sequence.
sources.note: Consolidation is editorial work over the published text. Where the wording is contested, the item as published in the Diário da República governs.

sources.name: Assembleia da Republica
sources.coverage: Bills (projetos de lei) and government bills (propostas de lei) with their stages, committee reports, plenary records and votes, by legislature
sources.desc: Where a statute is followed while it is still a bill, and where the reasoning is recorded. The exposição de motivos attached to a proposta de lei, and the committee report, are the standard materials for arguing what a provision was meant to achieve.
sources.howto: Use the legislative initiatives search filtered by legislature and type, and open an initiative to see its stages, the texts at each stage and the votes. The site also publishes the Constitution and the Assembly's rules in English under the EN section.
sources.note: Legislative authorisations to the Government are found here too, and they matter: a decreto-lei made outside the scope of its authorisation is unconstitutional.

sources.name: Tribunal Constitucional
sources.coverage: The Court's rulings and summary decisions, indexed by year and number, from its establishment in 1983 onward
sources.desc: A court with three distinct jurisdictions: preventive review at the President's request before a text is published, concrete review on appeal from any court that refused to apply a norm, and abstract review that can declare a norm unconstitutional with general binding force — a declaration published in the 1.ª série of the gazette.
sources.howto: Search by ruling number and year, by the norm at issue or by subject; decisions before 1998 are also in the DGSI database. Note which jurisdiction produced the decision: only a declaration with general binding force removes the norm for everyone.
sources.note: The Court also reviews unconstitutionality by omission — a finding that the legislature has failed to make a rule the Constitution requires, which is rarer and has no direct remedy.

sources.name: DGSI — bases juridico-documentais
sources.authority: Instituto de Gestão Financeira e Equipamentos da Justiça (IGFEJ), Ministry of Justice
sources.coverage: Separate databases per court, each with its document count on the front page: over 73,000 Supreme Court rulings, over 90,000 of the Supreme Administrative Court, more than 60,000 each from the Porto and Lisbon appeal courts, plus Coimbra, Guimarães and Évora, the Tribunal dos Conflitos, and opinions of the Attorney General
sources.desc: The free national case-law collection, organised as one database per court rather than one search across them. It is where Portuguese case law is actually looked up, and the counts on its front page are an honest statement of how much of each court's output is there.
sources.howto: Pick the court's database, then search by descriptors, case number, date or full text; the record gives the rapporteur, the descriptors and the full text. Constitutional Court rulings up to 1998 are here; later ones are on the Court's own site.
sources.note: Publication is selective and the interface is dated, but this is the state's own collection — commercial services largely republish it.

sources.name: Supremo Tribunal de Justica
sources.coverage: The Court's own publications, its uniformising rulings, statistics and annual reports; the full judgment database is on DGSI
sources.desc: The top of the civil and criminal judicial pyramid. Its acórdãos de uniformização de jurisprudência settle conflicts between its own chambers and are published in the 1.ª série of the gazette; they are not binding precedent — the binding assento was struck down as unconstitutional in 1993 — but departing from one requires reasons.
sources.howto: Use the Court's own site for the uniformising rulings and its published material, and DGSI for the general run of judgments. A citation gives the process number and date rather than a report volume.
sources.note: The Supremo Tribunal Administrativo heads a separate administrative and tax jurisdiction, and the Tribunal de Contas a third; none of the three reviews the others.

sources.name: Tribunal de Contas
sources.coverage: Rulings, prior-approval decisions (visto), audit reports and its own doctrine on public contracts and public finance
sources.desc: A court, not an audit office, and the reason many Portuguese public contracts do not take effect when signed: contracts above a threshold require its prior visto. Its case law is the operative law of public procurement and public spending in practice.
sources.howto: Search the rulings and reports by year and subject; the prior-approval decisions are published separately from the audit reports and are the ones that determine whether a contract can be performed.
sources.note: Its jurisdiction is financial. A contract refused a visto is not annulled as such, but it cannot produce financial effects.

sources.name: PGD Lisboa — base de dados legislativa
sources.native: Procuradoria-Geral Distrital de Lisboa — base de dados
sources.en: Legislation and case-law database of the Lisbon Prosecution Office
sources.coverage: Consolidated legislation with annotations, case law of the Lisbon appeal court, procedural precedents and interventions of the public prosecutor
sources.desc: A public prosecution office's own database that became, by accident of usefulness, one of the most consulted legal sites in Portugal. Its annotated codes — with case law and cross-references beneath each article — are frequently more usable than the official consolidated texts.
sources.howto: Open a code from the legislation index and read article by article; the annotations under an article gather the decisions and related provisions. Check the update date on the diploma before relying on the wording.
sources.note: Maintained by a state body but not an official publication: the texts are editorial consolidations and the annotations are the office's own. For the binding wording, return to the Diário da República.

sources.name: Jornal Oficial dos Acores
sources.native: Jornal Oficial da Região Autónoma dos Açores
sources.coverage: The regional gazette in its series, with the archive of past issues
sources.desc: The Azores have their own legislative assembly, and its decretos legislativos regionais are law in the region within the matters the Constitution and the political-administrative statute assign to it. They are published in the Diário da República as well, but regional regulations and administrative acts appear only here.
sources.howto: Browse by series and date or search the archive; regional legislative decrees can also be found in the national gazette by filtering the 1.ª série for the region.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: JORAM (Madeira)
sources.native: Jornal Oficial da Região Autónoma da Madeira
sources.coverage: The regional gazette in its series, with an archive of past issues
sources.desc: Madeira's equivalent, and the same principle: a regional legislative decree is law in the region, and the regional administration's acts and regulations are published here rather than nationally.
sources.howto: Browse issues by series and date, or search; the regional legislative assembly's own site carries the initiatives behind the diplomas.
sources.note: Regional legislation must respect the Constitution and cannot invade the Assembly's or the Government's reserved competences; the Constitutional Court decides where the line runs.

sources.name: Constitution in English (Assembleia)
sources.native: Constitution of the Portuguese Republic — seventh revision
sources.coverage: The full constitutional text as it stood after the seventh revision of 2005
sources.desc: The Assembly's own English text of the Constitution — effectively the only substantial piece of Portuguese law the state publishes in English.
sources.howto: Read or download the PDF; the Portuguese consolidated text on the DRE is the one to check any wording against.
sources.note: A translation, with no legal force, and tied to the 2005 revision rather than updated continuously.

sources.name: dados.gov.pt
sources.coverage: Public sector datasets, including judicial statistics and datasets published by the Ministry of Justice and other bodies
sources.desc: The state's open-data portal, which is where structured legal and judicial data is published when it is published at all — the gazette itself does not offer a public API.
sources.howto: Search the catalogue by publisher or subject; datasets vary in format and update frequency, and each record names the body responsible.
sources.note: Datasets, not legal texts. Nothing here is a source of law.

sources.name: EUR-Lex (em portugues)
sources.authority: Serviço das Publicações da União Europeia (Publications Office of the European Union)
sources.coverage: EU treaties, legislation, consolidated texts, case law and national implementing measures, in Portuguese among the official languages
sources.desc: Article 8 of the Constitution brings EU law into the internal order, and regulations apply without any Portuguese diploma. The Diário da República does not carry them, so this is the other half of the map.
sources.howto: Search by CELEX number or subject with the interface set to Portuguese; the national implementing measures tab on a directive lists the Portuguese diplomas notified for it.
sources.note: The Portuguese language version of an EU act is authentic alongside the others; the Official Journal edition is the binding one.

sources.name: Tratados no Diario da Republica
sources.native: Convenções internacionais — Diário da República, 1.ª série
sources.authority: Ministério dos Negócios Estrangeiros; published by Imprensa Nacional-Casa da Moeda
sources.coverage: Treaties and conventions with the resolution of the Assembly or the decree of the President approving them, and the notices of entry into force, all in the 1.ª série
sources.desc: Portugal has no separate treaty series: a convention is published in the 1.ª série of the gazette together with the instrument that approved it, and Article 8 of the Constitution makes a duly ratified convention part of the internal order once it is officially published and while it binds the state internationally.
sources.howto: Search the 1.ª série filtering the type of diploma to 'Resolução da Assembleia da República' or 'Decreto do Presidente da República' and the subject to the convention's name; then look for the later aviso announcing the date of entry into force, which is a separate item and is the date that matters.
sources.note: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' own treaty database is frequently unreachable from outside Portugal, which is why the gazette is given here as the route.

sources.name: Provedor de Justica
sources.authority: Provedor de Justiça, an independent officer elected by the Assembly
sources.coverage: Recommendations, opinions and annual reports, and the requests the Ombudsman has made to the Constitutional Court for abstract review
sources.desc: One of the few bodies that can put a norm before the Constitutional Court in abstract review without a case, which makes its published recommendations an early indicator of provisions that may not survive. It is also Portugal's national human rights institution.
sources.howto: Browse the recommendations and the requests for review by year and subject; each names the diploma and the provisions at issue, which is the fastest route into the constitutional argument about them.
sources.note: A recommendation binds nobody. Its significance is that it often precedes a change in the law or a ruling striking a provision down.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a diploma
findLaw.steps: Search the Diário da República for the diploma by number and year or by title, open it, and take the consolidated version if one is offered. If none is, note the amending diplomas listed on the page and read them in order — many minor diplomas have never been consolidated.

findLaw.task: Read the diploma exactly as published
findLaw.steps: Filter the search to the 1.ª série and the publication date, and open the item; the PDF of the issue is the published record. The series matters: if the text you want is in the 2.ª série, it is an administrative act rather than legislation.

findLaw.task: Work out when a rule starts to apply
findLaw.steps: Read the final articles of the diploma for its entry-into-force provision. Where it fixes none, the default is the fifth day after publication in the mainland, with longer periods for the autonomous regions and for Portuguese abroad — so publication date and effective date are usually different.

Choose the court's database on DGSI and search by descriptors, process number or date. For Constitutional Court rulings from 1998 onward use the Court's own site; for uniformising rulings of the Supreme Court, look both at the Court's site and in the 1.ª série of the gazette, where they are published.

findLaw.task: Check whether a provision has been struck down
findLaw.steps: Search the Constitutional Court's rulings for the norm. A declaration of unconstitutionality with general binding force is published in the 1.ª série and removes the norm for everyone, usually from the date it entered into force; a decision in concrete review binds only that case, even though it is often the better-known one.

findLaw.task: Find law that applies only in the Azores or Madeira
findLaw.steps: Regional legislative decrees are published in the Diário da República as well as in the region's own journal, so start with a filtered search of the 1.ª série. For regional regulations, administrative acts and everything below decree level, go to the Jornal Oficial of the region — they appear nowhere else.

Open the code on the Lisbon prosecution office's database, where each article carries the case law and cross-references beneath it. Treat it as a finding aid: check the wording against the consolidated text on the Diário da República before relying on it.
findLaw.source: PGD Lisboa — base de dados legislativa

subnational: Portugal is a unitary state with two autonomous regions and no other tier that legislates. The Azores and Madeira each have a legislative assembly whose decretos legislativos regionais have the force of law within the region, in the matters listed in their political-administrative statutes and not reserved to the national organs; these are published both in the Diário da República and in the region's own official journal, the Jornal Oficial da Região Autónoma dos Açores or JORAM. Regional regulations and administrative acts appear only in the regional journal. On the mainland the administrative regions provided for in the Constitution were never created, so below the state there are only municipalities and parishes, whose regulamentos and posturas are published by the municipality itself — in the municipal edital, on the municipal site and, for some, in the 2.ª série of the national gazette — and are not gathered in any national database.
caveats: The consolidated texts on the Diário da República are editorial work over the published item, and not every diploma has one: for older or minor legislation you may have to reconstruct the current wording from the original and each amendment in turn. The distinction between the two series is load-bearing — a text in the 2.ª série is an administrative act, not legislation — and so is the date: a diploma that fixes no date takes effect on the fifth day after publication in the mainland, later in the regions. Constitutional Court decisions come in kinds that do very different things, and only a declaration with general binding force removes a norm for everyone. DGSI publishes what the courts send it, which is selective, and its interface is old enough that a search can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with whether the decision exists. The Lisbon prosecution office's database is widely used and is not an official publication. The English text of the Constitution is a translation tied to the 2005 revision, and there is no official English version of Portuguese legislation generally.
